id_and_class.summary: Alexius Meinong splits every experience into a mental act, an immanent content that carries its phenomenal character, and an object the act is directed at, which need not exist at all. Consciousness can therefore be about golden mountains and round squares as readily as about real things. A state is conscious because it is self-presenting: it is directly available to its subject when the subject turns to it, without any higher-order thought or inner perception.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as Self-Presenting Directedness Toward Any Object

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is intentional directedness carried by real mental contents, open to objects of any status (existent, possible, fictional, incomplete, impossible), and made conscious by its self-presentation to the subject.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Not addressed. Meinong does not say how experience relates to the brain.
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Every act has an object as well as a content, even when the object has no being. Self-presentation lets an experience be grasped by its subject on reflection, but Meinong denies that every conscious act already includes explicit awareness of oneself as its subject.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Phenomenal character lies in the content, the qualitative material present in the experience and the part that determines which object the act targets. Imagining a red triangle and a blue circle differ phenomenally through their contents, which must not be confused with the figures intended.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Mental acts and real immanent contents; objects that exist, subsist, or are ‘outside being’; objects of higher order (melodies, shapes, relations) founded on simpler ones; objectives, the proposition-like objects of judgments and assumptions.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Descriptive psychology and self-presentation, which makes experiences directly graspable on reflection. Meinong also founded Austria-Hungary's first psychology laboratory at Graz in 1894.
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Act, content, object. Act types include presentation, assumption (entertaining a content without conviction, as in play or fiction), judgment, feeling, and desire.

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Intentionality; phenomenal content; what makes a state conscious; complex perception; affective consciousness.
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Self-presentation as a dispositional openness of the state to its subject, a third option beside higher-order and same-order theories that avoids a regress without positing a second act.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: Consciousness discloses objects without creating them. Emotions present values (dignitatives) and desires present desideratives, so affect is itself object-directed.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: Objects of higher order such as a melody or shape are founded on elementary objects, and representing them requires an active operation, the production of representations (Vorstellungsproduktion).
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: The mind produces complex representations, not complex objects. Contents are real parts of experience, not images or sense-data.
core_claims_and_evidence: Separating content from object, prompted by Twardowski, resolves Brentano's instability over whether intentional objects are literally in the mind.
Under the independence of being-so (Sosein) from being (Sein), an object can be round and square while lacking existence or subsistence.
Conscious experiences are self-presenting, available to the subject without higher-order thought or Brentanian inner perception.
Complex perceptual wholes are produced by operations on elementary contents, a thesis his student Vittorio Benussi tested experimentally at Graz.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Descriptive psychology and conceptual analysis, with early experimental work from the Graz School.

empirics_and_critiques.known_empirical_interventions_or_tests: Experimental work on production theory by Vittorio Benussi and the Graz School, which links to contemporary research on binding.
empirics_and_critiques.criticisms_and_tensions: Bertrand Russell's theory of descriptions offered an analysis of non-referring expressions without non-existent objects, and his criticism pushed Meinong out of analytic philosophy for decades. The overpopulated ‘Meinongian jungle’, a nickname probably due to William Kneale, was derided by Russellian and Rylean critics.
empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: Meinong does not explain why intentional activity is experienced phenomenally, how phenomenal unity is generated, or how experience relates to the brain.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Neo-Meinongian logics show that theories of non-existent objects can be formally coherent, though whether they are needed is disputed. The content/object split still frames debates on whether phenomenal character supervenes on representational content.
